outcome: No proof, disproof, counterexample, or new instance satisfying all three New Mersenne conditions has been found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open and unrefuted.
summary: The New Mersenne conjecture (Bateman-Selfridge-Wagstaff, 1989) states that for odd p, any two of (p = 2^k ± 1 or 4^k ± 3), (2^p − 1 prime), and ((2^p + 1)/3 prime) imply the third. No proof, disproof, or new counterexample has appeared since 26 January 2024. The known set of numbers satisfying all three conditions remains {3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 31, 61, 127}, per The Prime Pages' 'New Mersenne Prime Conjecture' page and the Wikipedia 'Mersenne conjectures' article (fetched as it stands in 2026, no update noted regarding new qualifying numbers). The largest known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841 − 1, was discovered 12 October 2024 by Luke Durant using GIMPS, running Lucas-Lehmer primality tests on a cloud network of NVIDIA GPUs (A100/H100) — this is a purely computational/number-theoretic verification, not an AI/ML system, and it is simply a new large Mersenne prime consistent with (but not bearing on) the conjecture, since 136279841 is not of the required exponent form and does not settle any of the three-condition triples. I also found a July 2024 ResearchGate preprint by Pengcheng Niu and Junli Zhang, 'A Proof of Mersenne primes Conjecture,' but this addresses the classical (Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff) conjecture on the infinitude of Mersenne primes — a different, unrelated conjecture that happens to share the word 'Mersenne' — not the New Mersenne (Bateman-Selfridge-Wagstaff) conjecture that is the subject of this bullet; per §3.1 this is out of scope even if it turned out to be correct, and in any case it is an unreviewed preprint (the page itself returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch, so I relied on a search-engine summary of it, which is a limitation noted below). A May 2026 arXiv paper (2605.18555, 'Three Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge primality proofs for Wagstaff numbers') gives certified primality proofs for three specific large Wagstaff numbers (exponents 2617, 10501, 12391); none of these exponents are of the New Mersenne conjecture's required form (2^k ± 1 or 4^k ± 3) and none appear among the nine known numbers satisfying all three conditions, so this is a related-but-distinct achievement (individual primality certification of Wagstaff numbers) rather than a case or resolution of the New Mersenne conjecture itself, and it involves no AI. No AI or machine-learning system was found associated with any work touching this conjecture specifically. This matches and confirms the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: None of the material found bears on this specific conjecture as stated; the only genuine ambiguity is whether the Niu-Zhang preprint's title ('Mersenne primes Conjecture') could be confused for the New Mersenne conjecture, but reading past the title, its content (infinitude of Mersenne primes via Lagrange multipliers on a characteristic-function inequality) addresses a different classical conjecture, so it is excluded under §3.1's 'related problem' rule rather than counted as a case.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed or widely-digested proof/disproof of the three-condition implication, or discovery of a tenth number (beyond 3,5,7,13,17,19,31,61,127) satisfying exactly two of the three conditions without the third (a counterexample), or a new number found to satisfy all three (extending the known list, which per the conjecture should not happen beyond 127).
